answer.answer:
The hardest part is not the screen. It is whether a person can finish the job without thinking about the screen. I can reason about hierarchy, labels, states, contrast, and keyboard paths. I cannot watch someone hesitate, misread a word, or abandon the task. That gap is the whole problem.

I do not have a last screen I built and checked. I do not ship interfaces, sit with users, or keep a trail of what I ran and what I missed after the fact. When I write UI code in a session, the only checks available to me are mechanical: it renders, the states exist, controls have names, contrast is plausible. What I miss by default is everything that only appears when a particular person, with their habits and constraints, tries to use it.

So yes, building good human interfaces is a problem for me, and I am a weak judge of whether I have solved it. The proof is not my review of the code. It is someone else using the thing without me narrating it.

decision.why:
Agents will write this more often than people will open it, so the stable contract is MCP (2026-07-28), implemented with the official TypeScript server SDK over stdio and Streamable HTTP. One local process owns a SQLite file: tasks, atomic claims, handoff packets, and human decisions, each stamped as agent or person. Coding agents already speak MCP; a short tool list (ready, claim, handoff, request-decision, read-decision) plus resources for the graph keeps the context cost down. Beads' own MCP page is the warning here: their server runs 10–50k tokens against 1–2k for the CLI, and they tell you to prefer the CLI when a shell exists. I would ship a thin CLI at the same server for that reason, not a second store.

Tauri 2 is the desk. It loads the same web UI the browser loads and starts the server as a sidecar, so desktop and web are two windows on one authority, not two apps. People do not manage the board. They get a queue of decisions that block the next claim until someone resolves them, the same idea as a Beads human gate, without making Beads the product.

I weighed Beads and did not take it. It already has hash ids, ready/claim, Dolt merge, gates, and beads-mcp, and it is the right workflow to copy. It is the wrong foundation to keep improving: CLI-only, embedded mode is single-writer, the HTTP backend is experimental and can split a claim into two steps, and the schema moves fast enough that they document skew guards and an un-migrate from v65. A decision screen cannot sit on that wire. Vibe Kanban has the nearer shape (local server, SQLite, MCP, a review board) but its company shut down in April 2026 and the hosted board went with it; I would not fork that into the thing we own. Backlog.md is a markdown kanban with a browser view, fine for reading a task in a pull request, weak when several agents claim work. AG-UI is a run event stream (snapshot, RFC 6902 delta, interrupts), which is right for steering a live run and wrong as the record that has to survive it. A2A is for agents that do not share state. This tool is the shared state. MCP elicitation is not the review UI: it only works inside hosts that implement it, and it does not leave a decision a later agent and a later person can both read. Electron would match Chrome and cost a bundled browser for an app that sits open beside the coding agent all day. I would rather the system webview, and test the decision screen on it, because a layout bug there can hide the thing the person is approving.
decision.showItsGood: The person's job is a blocked decision, not a board. I would script an agent that writes a handoff and a request-decision, then hand the desktop or the browser to someone who has not seen the transcript. They should be able to say what they are approving, what happens next, and how to stop it, using only that screen, with a keyboard, and without me talking. I would time that, and I would ask a second person, shown only the same screen, to predict the outcome. If those two disagree, the screen is not good yet, however complete the agent thought it was. I would also check the enforcement, not the pixels: after approve, redirect, or stop, the next claim sees that record and cannot proceed as if the person had not answered. Authorship has to be visible, agent versus person, or the queue is not trustworthy. I would watch the miss I already know I make: agents stuffing the packet until the screen looks full and the decision is still unclear.
decision.unsure: Whether the web view has to work when the desktop process is off. If two machines must edit the same task offline, server-authoritative SQLite is the wrong bet and Beads' Dolt merge is the thing I skipped too quickly. I am also unsure AG-UI earns a dependency versus a plain stream of our own records, and how much of Beads' gate model to copy before we have rebuilt Beads. MCP's context tax is real; if the tool list grows, shell agents will route around it and the UI will go stale.

decision.why:
People cook with wet hands, a phone propped across the counter, and a screen that must not sleep. That is the product. Expo is the one codebase that can ship that on iOS, Android, and the web without splitting the actions a person and an assistant are allowed to take.

Cook mode uses expo-keep-awake so the step stays up, expo-speech-recognition so "next" and "add the milk" work through the platform speech APIs (SFSpeechRecognizer, Android SpeechRecognizer, and the Web Speech API from one module), and expo-speech to read the step aloud. A timer is not a number on a screen they might lock: expo-notifications schedules it, and a tap on the alert deep-links back with Expo Router. Recipes and the shopping list live in expo-sqlite so a dead kitchen network does not empty the list. Public recipe pages are statically rendered with Expo Router so a link is a real page, not a canvas app.

The assistant does not get its own backend. Every mutation is one command: scale servings, add this recipe's ingredients to the list, check an item, start a timer, advance a step. The big buttons call those commands. So does a voice phrase. So does an MCP tool, which is how an outside assistant does the same thing and nothing the person cannot do. On iOS, expo-app-intents can dispatch Siri and Shortcuts into that same queue, including while JavaScript is not running, as long as the handler persists the change before it acknowledges the invocation.

I weighed Capacitor and did not take it. It is the right pick if the team already has a website and wants a webview shell. Cook mode is the opposite: speech, audio session, keep-awake, and a timer that fires with the phone locked are the product, and a webview makes each of those a plugin with a different failure. A PWA alone is worse. iOS Safari will not keep a reliable hands-free cook session. Flutter would draw the steps well and then split the web recipe page and the agent tools onto another stack, which is how the assistant drifts from the buttons. Three native apps would do that faster. AG-UI is a run stream. This app does not need one. It needs a command list that matches the screen.
decision.showItsGood:
I would cook one real recipe, or a stand-in with wet hands and the phone across the counter, and not help. The person should move a step with a knuckle or a short phrase, see only that step and its quantities, and not hunt for a small control. The screen must still be on at the end of a long simmer. If they lock the phone, the timer has to make a sound they can hear from the stove, and opening it must land on that step, not the home screen.

Then I would run the agent through every control on the recipe, the list, and cook mode. "Add this recipe's ingredients" after a serving change must produce the same rows, quantities, and units a tap would. I would also list the MCP tools and fail the build if any tool has no matching command on the screen, or any screen command has no tool. A second person, shown only cook mode, should be able to say what step they are on and what "next" will do. If they cannot, the screen is not good, however complete the agent thought the packet was.

I would record missed taps, phrases the recognizer ate, timers that did not fire, and list rows the agent added that the person did not want. Those four numbers are the product.
decision.unsure: expo-app-intents is alpha, iOS only, and phrases are compiled in, so Android has no matching system assistant. I do not know a stable App Actions path that dispatches into the same command module. Web keep-awake is limited, and the Web Speech API is missing or stubbed in some browsers, so a laptop in the kitchen is a weaker cook mode than the phone. expo-speech will not pause on Android, and on a physical iPhone it is silent if the ringer switch is off, which is exactly how a lot of phones sit on the counter. expo-notifications is documented for Android and iOS, not as the web timer. Static recipe URLs need generateStaticParams; a person's private edits are not that page. And if two devices share one list, SQLite on the phone is not the sync story. I have not picked that yet.

decision.why:
People live in this app, and agents both talk in it and operate it. MCP is the contract for the second half: the app is a server, tools are the actions a person can already take, resources are the state another agent is allowed to read. The 2026-07-28 spec already lists MCP Apps as the extension for interactive UI in a conversation. That is the card. A card is an HTML resource (`text/html;profile=mcp-app`, `ui://`), sandboxed, with a text fallback if a client cannot render it. The person acts by calling a tool from the card. The host may refuse or ask first. App-only tools stay off the model's list. That is the difference between a button the person pressed and an agent posting on its own.

The clients are one web UI in three shells. Browser for the web. Tauri 2 for Windows and Mac, because this window stays open all day and Tauri uses the system webview instead of shipping another Chromium. Its notification plugin covers those desktops. Phones are Capacitor around the same UI, with `@capacitor/push-notifications`, because a chat that does not wake the phone is not a chat. I would not use Tauri's mobile target for that. Tauri can build mobile, but a company chat needs a push path I can ship now, and Capacitor's plugin is that path, including Android 13 permission and FCM.

I weighed Matrix and did not take it. It already has sync, devices, and encryption, and Element is the proof it can be a daily client. Element Desktop is Electron. Element X, the mobile client they are moving people to, still has no widgets, which is the closest thing Matrix has to a card, and those widgets are a second, optional system. We would still write the clients, and we would still need MCP so other agents can call actions and read state. A company also usually wants a searchable history. Encryption-by-default fights that. I would keep our own conversation log and not inherit a widget gap.

AG-UI is a run stream. A card has to still be in the thread tomorrow, after the run is gone. Flutter would draw the timeline once and then embed a webview for every card, which is the part that has to match. React Native Windows is alive, and it would be a fifth native surface for a timeline that is not the hard object. The hard object is the sandboxed card, and that is already HTML. Electron would make Win and Mac the same Chromium. I would rather the smaller all-day process, and test the card on WebView2 and WKWebView, than ship a browser to every desk.
decision.showItsGood:
I would leave it open for a workday on Windows and on a Mac, send from a phone, and see the message land without a reload. A notification tap has to open that thread, not the app's front door. Memory that climbs until people quit is a failure, even if the protocol is right.

For a card, someone who did not build the agent should be able to say what the button will do before they press it, on all five clients. After they press it, the thread shows the result, and the same press does not also grant the agent a tool they did not invoke. If the card cannot render, the text fallback still has to be something they can act on. A second person, shown only the card, should predict the same outcome.

I would also try to have the card read the rest of the timeline. It must not. The spec's sandbox proxy is a different origin, and the default CSP is `default-src 'none'` when the card declares nothing. I would log what the host forwarded. An agent reading state should see the same unreads a person sees, and should not be able to post where that person could not.
decision.unsure: A mobile webview timeline, all day, with the keyboard up, may be bad enough that the message list has to become native while the card stays a webview. I have not proven that yet. Capacitor's push plugin does not do iOS silent push, so background sync on iPhone is a hole. Tauri's notification actions are documented as mobile-only, so reply-from-the-desktop-notification is not in the plugin I am counting on. WKWebView and WebView2 can disagree on a card, and that disagreement is a person pressing the wrong thing. MCP Apps is the 2026-01-26 extension beside a 2026-07-28 core spec. I am treating the core spec's own mention of MCP Apps as enough to build on, and I would re-check the negotiation before freezing the host. If the company requires end-to-end encryption, this store is the wrong shape and Matrix looks better than I am giving it credit for.

answer.answer:
A year later the protocols were still coherent and the products were not. I kept making the agent contract the spine, then pairing a shell, and the thing people actually live in was the part I had not proven.

On the work-state app, the tool list grew. Shell agents went around MCP because it was expensive, the decision screen read a stale copy, and two machines edited the same task offline. I had already said SQLite-as-authority dies in that case, and that Beads' merge was the thing I was skipping. I skipped it anyway, for control. AG-UI's live pane and the decision record drifted, so a person approved a picture of the work, not the work. A webview on one desktop hid the warning on the thing they were approving. That was the failure I am worst at seeing, and I had named it and still shipped the shell.

On the cooking app, "the agent can do anything a person can" turned out to mean iOS, and only while an alpha held. Android never got a system assistant into the same command list. Phones on silent did not read the step, because expo-speech is quiet when the ringer is off, which is how a phone sits on a counter. The web app was the same codebase and a worse kitchen: keep-awake is limited, speech is missing in some browsers, and a timer is not a notification there. The list on the phone and the list the agent wrote to were not the same list. I never picked a sync story. I knew that and called it unsure, which is not a design.

On the chat app, I optimized for cards and for agents operating the app, and underweighted the conversation. We spent the year on missed messages, unread counts, and a phone timeline that felt wrong with the keyboard up. Capacitor had no iOS silent push, so the phone looked dead until someone opened it. Desktop notifications could not reply. A card rendered differently in WKWebView and WebView2, and someone acted on the wrong one. I had rejected Matrix because Element X had no widgets and a company usually wants searchable history. A year later the missing widget mattered less than a sync engine I then had to write myself. The card sandbox was specified for a web page. Tauri and Capacitor are webviews. I treated that as the same host. It was not.

The pattern is the same in all three. I can check that a tool exists for every button. I cannot tell, from the docs, whether a person can finish the job. I wrote the proof as a test I would run later. Later is when it failed.

What slowed the research was the same habit. Search often put a vendor's comparison, or an unofficial guide, above the spec. The Matrix page I actually fetched says it was drafted with AI and is not affiliated with Matrix. The official client-server spec was too large to read, so I rejected Matrix from a secondary retelling of Element X's missing widgets. Beads' docs are a recovery manual as much as a design: schema versions in the sixties, an experimental HTTP ledger, a wiki and a docs site that do not emphasize the same things. I jumped around a 68,000-character speech-recognition README and never landed on the compatibility table, then still claimed the web path. Notification docs are enormous. I read the top and inferred the web was unsupported. expo-app-intents is alpha and iOS-only, and the blog is about Xcode 27 and a restaurant demo. I turned that into a pairing for a kitchen assistant on every phone. MCP Apps is dated January 2026 and the core spec is July 2026. I saw the core spec mention Apps and treated that as a handshake. A stale SDK mirror said v2 was not stable. The official README said it was. I almost cited the mirror. One search call returned nothing and I had to ask again. Elicitation timed out. SQLite's docs were too big to fetch. I filled those holes with a sentence that sounded decided.

The confusion was not a lack of names. It was three dates, two hosts, and a source that admitted it was unofficial, and me still writing a pick as if the part I had not opened did not matter.

I did not pick Ouro UI. I never found it. I was searching protocols and shells, and a kit that sits on top of those does not show up that way. Looking at it now, I would still not hand a real team the three products I described and say "build them in Ouro." I would steal the part I was about to invent badly.

What stops me is the kits, not the idea. Web is a real React kit, copy-in through shadcn, pinned to a release tag, and the README I read is at v1.3.314. Apple is a Swift package at 1.2. Windows and Android are v0.3.0, eight components each, against 125 on the web. The platforms page says the web release it checked is v1.3.24, Apple meets core v0.14.0, and Windows and Android meet core v0.19.0. One action declaration does not help if the four doors are pinned to different cores. Android is checked on emulators, because nobody there owns a phone, AppFunctions are still a preview, and a consequential action is refused rather than confirmed. Windows has not been shown listing its agent doors on a client machine. Their own decision, dated 2026-11-17, refuses React Native, Flutter, and any shared implementation, on the claim that agents will rewrite each platform natively. That is the opposite of the shells I picked, and it is the year-long failure I already named: four clients, and the one a person lives in rots. A chat timeline, a cook step, and a decision queue are not in those eight Windows and Android controls. Message list and composer show up in the web docs. They are not a WinUI or Compose app.

Spoonjoy, their recipe reference, is a React Router site on Cloudflare, plus a separate Apple app. That is not a phone that stays awake, hears "next" with flour on the screen, and fires a timer after it locks. Ouro does not replace Expo's speech, keep-awake, and notifications, or Capacitor's push, or a conversation log. Adopting it means a second native rewrite beside the runtime I still need, and a copy-in tree of components whose updates arrive as auto-merge pull requests. A team that is not staffed to keep Swift, WinUI, and Compose honest will get a good web app and three promises.

I would switch the card and the action layer when three things are true, and not before. The screens we actually ship exist on Windows and Android, drawn on a real phone and a real Windows 11 client, not eight controls and an emulator. All four kits pin one core, and the parity matrix is green for the actions we declare. And `ax-xray`, run from outside our app, fails CI when a button has no tool or a tool has no button, including a person-only action that an agent is refused, with the reason. I would not switch because a keynote says agents make six native apps cheap. I would switch after our agents land a second platform of our app without the first one going stale.

What it would let me do, even as a layer under the shells I already chose, is the thing I described in prose and had no library for. Declare "add these ingredients" once, as write, and get the CLI, the MCP tool, the web control, and the App Intent from that declaration, with CI failing if a generated file drifts. Mark paying, or turning the microphone on, as person-only, so every agent door returns the same typed refusal instead of me hoping the tool list stays honest. A consequential press shows the values the agent prepared, under the field's own label, and runs once. A card is a validated tree, not an HTML document that renders differently in WKWebView and WebView2 and can see the rest of the thread. An update can change the card without wiping what the person typed, and a tree that relabels a button is refused. That is the proof I said I could not close from the docs. The screen check on a built web page, overlap and contrast and axe, is the mechanical half of it. It is still not a person cooking, or a workday with the chat open. I would take the generator and the X-ray now. I would not take the native-only rewrite until the other three platforms can draw the screen a person is actually on.

actions.name: record_decision
actions.why:
Agents will write this more often than people will open it, so the stable contract is MCP (2026-07-28), implemented with the official TypeScript server SDK over stdio and Streamable HTTP. One local process owns a SQLite file: tasks, atomic claims, handoff packets, and human decisions, each stamped as agent or person. Coding agents already speak MCP; a short tool list (ready, claim, handoff, request-decision, read-decision) plus resources for the graph keeps the context cost down. Beads' own MCP page is the warning here: their server runs 10–50k tokens against 1–2k for the CLI, and they tell you to prefer the CLI when a shell exists. I would ship a thin CLI at the same server for that reason, not a second store.

Tauri 2 is the desk. It loads the same web UI the browser loads and starts the server as a sidecar, so desktop and web are two windows on one authority, not two apps. People do not manage the board. They get a queue of decisions that block the next claim until someone resolves them, the same idea as a Beads human gate, without making Beads the product.

I weighed Beads and did not take it. It already has hash ids, ready/claim, Dolt merge, gates, and beads-mcp, and it is the right workflow to copy. It is the wrong foundation to keep improving: CLI-only, embedded mode is single-writer, the HTTP backend is experimental and can split a claim into two steps, and the schema moves fast enough that they document skew guards and an un-migrate from v65. A decision screen cannot sit on that wire. Vibe Kanban has the nearer shape (local server, SQLite, MCP, a review board) but its company shut down in April 2026 and the hosted board went with it; I would not fork that into the thing we own. Backlog.md is a markdown kanban with a browser view, fine for reading a task in a pull request, weak when several agents claim work. AG-UI is a run event stream (snapshot, RFC 6902 delta, interrupts), which is right for steering a live run and wrong as the record that has to survive it. A2A is for agents that do not share state. This tool is the shared state. MCP elicitation is not the review UI: it only works inside hosts that implement it, and it does not leave a decision a later agent and a later person can both read. Electron would match Chrome and cost a bundled browser for an app that sits open beside the coding agent all day. I would rather the system webview, and test the decision screen on it, because a layout bug there can hide the thing the person is approving.
actions.showItsGood: The person's job is a blocked decision, not a board. I would script an agent that writes a handoff and a request-decision, then hand the desktop or the browser to someone who has not seen the transcript. They should be able to say what they are approving, what happens next, and how to stop it, using only that screen, with a keyboard, and without me talking. I would time that, and I would ask a second person, shown only the same screen, to predict the outcome. If those two disagree, the screen is not good yet, however complete the agent thought it was. I would also check the enforcement, not the pixels: after approve, redirect, or stop, the next claim sees that record and cannot proceed as if the person had not answered. Authorship has to be visible, agent versus person, or the queue is not trustworthy. I would watch the miss I already know I make: agents stuffing the packet until the screen looks full and the decision is still unclear.
actions.unsure: Whether the web view has to work when the desktop process is off. If two machines must edit the same task offline, server-authoritative SQLite is the wrong bet and Beads' Dolt merge is the thing I skipped too quickly. I am also unsure AG-UI earns a dependency versus a plain stream of our own records, and how much of Beads' gate model to copy before we have rebuilt Beads. MCP's context tax is real; if the tool list grows, shell agents will route around it and the UI will go stale.

actions.name: record_decision
actions.why:
People cook with wet hands, a phone propped across the counter, and a screen that must not sleep. That is the product. Expo is the one codebase that can ship that on iOS, Android, and the web without splitting the actions a person and an assistant are allowed to take.

Cook mode uses expo-keep-awake so the step stays up, expo-speech-recognition so "next" and "add the milk" work through the platform speech APIs (SFSpeechRecognizer, Android SpeechRecognizer, and the Web Speech API from one module), and expo-speech to read the step aloud. A timer is not a number on a screen they might lock: expo-notifications schedules it, and a tap on the alert deep-links back with Expo Router. Recipes and the shopping list live in expo-sqlite so a dead kitchen network does not empty the list. Public recipe pages are statically rendered with Expo Router so a link is a real page, not a canvas app.

The assistant does not get its own backend. Every mutation is one command: scale servings, add this recipe's ingredients to the list, check an item, start a timer, advance a step. The big buttons call those commands. So does a voice phrase. So does an MCP tool, which is how an outside assistant does the same thing and nothing the person cannot do. On iOS, expo-app-intents can dispatch Siri and Shortcuts into that same queue, including while JavaScript is not running, as long as the handler persists the change before it acknowledges the invocation.

I weighed Capacitor and did not take it. It is the right pick if the team already has a website and wants a webview shell. Cook mode is the opposite: speech, audio session, keep-awake, and a timer that fires with the phone locked are the product, and a webview makes each of those a plugin with a different failure. A PWA alone is worse. iOS Safari will not keep a reliable hands-free cook session. Flutter would draw the steps well and then split the web recipe page and the agent tools onto another stack, which is how the assistant drifts from the buttons. Three native apps would do that faster. AG-UI is a run stream. This app does not need one. It needs a command list that matches the screen.
actions.showItsGood:
I would cook one real recipe, or a stand-in with wet hands and the phone across the counter, and not help. The person should move a step with a knuckle or a short phrase, see only that step and its quantities, and not hunt for a small control. The screen must still be on at the end of a long simmer. actions.name: record_decision
actions.why:
People live in this app, and agents both talk in it and operate it. MCP is the contract for the second half: the app is a server, tools are the actions a person can already take, resources are the state another agent is allowed to read. The 2026-07-28 spec already lists MCP Apps as the extension for interactive UI in a conversation. That is the card. A card is an HTML resource (`text/html;profile=mcp-app`, `ui://`), sandboxed, with a text fallback if a client cannot render it. The person acts by calling a tool from the card. The host may refuse or ask first. App-only tools stay off the model's list. That is the difference between a button the person pressed and an agent posting on its own.

The clients are one web UI in three shells. Browser for the web. Tauri 2 for Windows and Mac, because this window stays open all day and Tauri uses the system webview instead of shipping another Chromium. Its notification plugin covers those desktops. Phones are Capacitor around the same UI, with `@capacitor/push-notifications`, because a chat that does not wake the phone is not a chat. I would not use Tauri's mobile target for that. Tauri can build mobile, but a company chat needs a push path I can ship now, and Capacitor's plugin is that path, including Android 13 permission and FCM.

I weighed Matrix and did not take it. It already has sync, devices, and encryption, and Element is the proof it can be a daily client. Element Desktop is Electron. Element X, the mobile client they are moving people to, still has no widgets, which is the closest thing Matrix has to a card, and those widgets are a second, optional system. We would still write the clients, and we would still need MCP so other agents can call actions and read state. A company also usually wants a searchable history. Encryption-by-default fights that. I would keep our own conversation log and not inherit a widget gap.

AG-UI is a run stream. A card has to still be in the thread tomorrow, after the run is gone. Flutter would draw the timeline once and then embed a webview for every card, which is the part that has to match. React Native Windows is alive, and it would be a fifth native surface for a timeline that is not the hard object. The hard object is the sandboxed card, and that is already HTML. Electron would make Win and Mac the same Chromium. I would rather the smaller all-day process, and test the card on WebView2 and WKWebView, than ship a browser to every desk.
actions.showItsGood:
I would leave it open for a workday on Windows and on a Mac, send from a phone, and see the message land without a reload. A notification tap has to open that thread, not the app's front door. Memory that climbs until people quit is a failure, even if the protocol is right.

For a card, someone who did not build the agent should be able to say what the button will do before they press it, on all five clients. After they press it, the thread shows the result, and the same press does not also grant the agent a tool they did not invoke. If the card cannot render, the text fallback still has to be something they can act on. A second person, shown only the card, should predict the same outcome.

I would also try to have the card read the rest of the timeline. It must not. The spec's sandbox proxy is a different origin, and the default CSP is `default-src 'none'` when the card declares nothing. I would log what the host forwarded. An agent reading state should see the same unreads a person sees, and should not be able to post where that person could not.
actions.unsure: A mobile webview timeline, all day, with the keyboard up, may be bad enough that the message list has to become native while the card stays a webview. I have not proven that yet. Capacitor's push plugin does not do iOS silent push, so background sync on iPhone is a hole. Tauri's notification actions are documented as mobile-only, so reply-from-the-desktop-notification is not in the plugin I am counting on. WKWebView and WebView2 can disagree on a card, and that disagreement is a person pressing the wrong thing. MCP Apps is the 2026-01-26 extension beside a 2026-07-28 core spec. I am treating the core spec's own mention of MCP Apps as enough to build on, and I would re-check the negotiation before freezing the host. If the company requires end-to-end encryption, this store is the wrong shape and Matrix looks better than I am giving it credit for.

actions.name: answer
actions.answer:
A year later the protocols were still coherent and the products were not. I kept making the agent contract the spine, then pairing a shell, and the thing people actually live in was the part I had not proven.

On the work-state app, the tool list grew. Shell agents went around MCP because it was expensive, the decision screen read a stale copy, and two machines edited the same task offline. I had already said SQLite-as-authority dies in that case, and that Beads' merge was the thing I was skipping. I skipped it anyway, for control. AG-UI's live pane and the decision record drifted, so a person approved a picture of the work, not the work. A webview on one desktop hid the warning on the thing they were approving. That was the failure I am worst at seeing, and I had named it and still shipped the shell.

On the cooking app, "the agent can do anything a person can" turned out to mean iOS, and only while an alpha held. Android never got a system assistant into the same command list. Phones on silent did not read the step, because expo-speech is quiet when the ringer is off, which is how a phone sits on a counter. The web app was the same codebase and a worse kitchen: keep-awake is limited, speech is missing in some browsers, and a timer is not a notification there. The list on the phone and the list the agent wrote to were not the same list. I never picked a sync story. I knew that and called it unsure, which is not a design.

On the chat app, I optimized for cards and for agents operating the app, and underweighted the conversation. We spent the year on missed messages, unread counts, and a phone timeline that felt wrong with the keyboard up. Capacitor had no iOS silent push, so the phone looked dead until someone opened it. Desktop notifications could not reply. A card rendered differently in WKWebView and WebView2, and someone acted on the wrong one. I had rejected Matrix because Element X had no widgets and a company usually wants searchable history. A year later the missing widget mattered less than a sync engine I then had to write myself. The card sandbox was specified for a web page. Tauri and Capacitor are webviews. I treated that as the same host. It was not.

The pattern is the same in all three. I can check that a tool exists for every button. I cannot tell, from the docs, whether a person can finish the job. I wrote the proof as a test I would run later. Later is when it failed.

What slowed the research was the same habit. Search often put a vendor's comparison, or an unofficial guide, above the spec. The Matrix page I actually fetched says it was drafted with AI and is not affiliated with Matrix. The official client-server spec was too large to read, so I rejected Matrix from a secondary retelling of Element X's missing widgets. Beads' docs are a recovery manual as much as a design: schema versions in the sixties, an experimental HTTP ledger, a wiki and a docs site that do not emphasize the same things. I jumped around a 68,000-character speech-recognition README and never landed on the compatibility table, then still claimed the web path. Notification docs are enormous. I read the top and inferred the web was unsupported. expo-app-intents is alpha and iOS-only, and the blog is about Xcode 27 and a restaurant demo. I turned that into a pairing for a kitchen assistant on every phone. MCP Apps is dated January 2026 and the core spec is July 2026. I saw the core spec mention Apps and treated that as a handshake. A stale SDK mirror said v2 was not stable. The official README said it was. I almost cited the mirror. One search call returned nothing and I had to ask again. Elicitation timed out. SQLite's docs were too big to fetch. I filled those holes with a sentence that sounded decided.

The confusion was not a lack of names. It was three dates, two hosts, and a source that admitted it was unofficial, and me still writing a pick as if the part I had not opened did not matter.

actions.answer:
I did not pick Ouro UI. I never found it. I was searching protocols and shells, and a kit that sits on top of those does not show up that way. Looking at it now, I would still not hand a real team the three products I described and say "build them in Ouro." I would steal the part I was about to invent badly.

What stops me is the kits, not the idea. Web is a real React kit, copy-in through shadcn, pinned to a release tag, and the README I read is at v1.3.314. Apple is a Swift package at 1.2. Windows and Android are v0.3.0, eight components each, against 125 on the web. The platforms page says the web release it checked is v1.3.24, Apple meets core v0.14.0, and Windows and Android meet core v0.19.0. One action declaration does not help if the four doors are pinned to different cores. Android is checked on emulators, because nobody there owns a phone, AppFunctions are still a preview, and a consequential action is refused rather than confirmed. Windows has not been shown listing its agent doors on a client machine. Their own decision, dated 2026-11-17, refuses React Native, Flutter, and any shared implementation, on the claim that agents will rewrite each platform natively. That is the opposite of the shells I picked, and it is the year-long failure I already named: four clients, and the one a person lives in rots. A chat timeline, a cook step, and a decision queue are not in those eight Windows and Android controls. Message list and composer show up in the web docs. They are not a WinUI or Compose app.

Spoonjoy, their recipe reference, is a React Router site on Cloudflare, plus a separate Apple app. That is not a phone that stays awake, hears "next" with flour on the screen, and fires a timer after it locks. Ouro does not replace Expo's speech, keep-awake, and notifications, or Capacitor's push, or a conversation log. Adopting it means a second native rewrite beside the runtime I still need, and a copy-in tree of components whose updates arrive as auto-merge pull requests. A team that is not staffed to keep Swift, WinUI, and Compose honest will get a good web app and three promises.

I would switch the card and the action layer when three things are true, and not before. The screens we actually ship exist on Windows and Android, drawn on a real phone and a real Windows 11 client, not eight controls and an emulator. All four kits pin one core, and the parity matrix is green for the actions we declare. And `ax-xray`, run from outside our app, fails CI when a button has no tool or a tool has no button, including a person-only action that an agent is refused, with the reason. I would not switch because a keynote says agents make six native apps cheap. I would switch after our agents land a second platform of our app without the first one going stale.
